issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal of feared uncontrollable rage is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no corresponding trigger, threat, memory, or strategy items suggesting anger-driven reactivity, aggression risk, or conflict; the other appraisals instead center on shame and hopelessness after rape. This makes the rage item clinically discordant within the selected five components.

issues.item: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
issues.explanation: The strategy of constant socialising is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile in this rape-related presentation. The selected triggers are solitary/sensory reminders (silence, outdoor smells, anniversary), and the appraisals are shame, suicidality, and feared rage. Constantly surrounding oneself with people does not connect clearly to these reminders and is somewhat at odds with body shame after rape, making it the least coherent avoidance/coping item here.

vignette:
# Abigail's Story

Abigail was seventy-four when she came to the clinic, her hands bearing the deep creases and weathered brown of a lifetime spent in soil. She had worked the fields of North Carolina since she was a girl—tobacco first, then vegetables, seasonal work that had sustained her through decades of marriage and loss. Three years ago, on a warm evening in April, a man had emerged from the rows of early spring crops while she was securing equipment near the barn. She had been alone, the sky already darkening, the smell of turned earth still thick in the air from the day's planting. What happened in those minutes had fractured something in her that she had not yet named when she sat across from the therapist, only that the world had become a place where she no longer recognized herself.

The anniversary came around each April, and with it came a particular dread that lodged in her chest weeks before the date arrived. She found herself counting down the days, unable to stop the arithmetic of her own suffering. But it was not only the calendar that haunted her. The smell of soil—that rich, organic scent that had once been the smell of honest work and provision—had become something else entirely. When the season turned and she was required to work the fields, the moment that smell reached her was the moment her body would go rigid, her breathing shallow, as though the air itself had become dangerous. She had come to believe that the earth itself held something of what had been done to her, that it was contaminated with her shame in a way she could not articulate but could not escape.

Silence, too, had become an enemy. The quiet of the early morning before work began, the silence of the house after her partner left for town, the sudden absence of sound—these moments would leave her suspended in a kind of terror, her mind rushing to fill the void with the memory of her own muted cries. She had begun leaving the radio on constantly, the television murmuring through the day, anything to keep the silence at bay.

What had begun as a necessary caution had slowly become a prison. Abigail had stopped going into the fields at dusk. Then she stopped going when it was dark at all. Then, without quite deciding to, she began to avoid the circumstances of work itself—making excuses, claiming illness, until her employer had quietly reassigned her to lighter indoor tasks. The loss of her place in the fields, the work that had defined her, had left a hollow ache that she could not separate from the shame that consumed her.

The physical contact was perhaps the cruelest consequence. Her partner, Marcus, had been patient for months, but his patience had worn thin in a way that neither of them spoke about directly. When he reached for her hand, she would find her body recoiling before her mind could catch up. When he tried to hold her at night, she would stiffen, her skin burning with a sensation she could only describe as filth—not dirt, but something deeper, something that no amount of washing could remove. She felt contaminated in a way that extended beyond her body; she had come to believe that she carried something poisoned, that her very presence might transfer it to him. It was easier to turn away, to excuse herself, to sleep in the other room. The distance between them had grown into something neither of them knew how to bridge.

In recent weeks, a new thought had begun to visit her with increasing frequency: that the life she was living was no longer worth the effort of living it. She was not actively suicidal, but she had stopped watering the plants on her porch, had begun to let small tasks accumulate. It was this thought, whispered to Marcus one evening, that had finally moved him to insist she seek help. Abigail had come to the clinic because she could no longer bear the weight of what she was carrying alone, though she arrived uncertain whether healing was even possible for someone as damaged as she believed herself to be.
